title: Vendor Risk and Portability — Module Quiz

items.q: Which layer of dependency do people most often leave off a dependency diagram?
options: The model provider
The people: who holds the keys and who can recover an account
The database
items.explain: People are the dependency most often missing from the diagram and the one that most often fails.

items.q: What are the three time horizons to ask of each dependency?
options: An hour, a day and a month
A day, a week and gone for good
A week, a month and a year
items.explain: The first usually means some inconvenience, the second often reveals a real cost, and the third is where the planning belongs.

items.q: Why rank dependencies by consequence rather than likelihood?
options: Likelihood cannot be estimated
A rare event with catastrophic consequences still deserves a plan, whatever the odds
Consequence is easier to measure
items.explain: Spend attention where the consequence is high, and give routine defences to the common but moderate failures.

items.q: What does inheriting the dependencies of your dependencies mean in practice?
options: You must audit every vendor's suppliers
Your host, libraries and provider rely on other services you never chose, and their failures become yours
Vendors are legally responsible for their suppliers' failures to you
items.explain: You cannot map everything, but each failure reveals a dependency you had not drawn, so revisit the map when something breaks.

items.q: What does a free tier usually promise?
options: The same availability as a paid plan
Very little: no service commitment, and a limit or term that can change or end
A guaranteed upgrade path at the same price
items.explain: Build on it with open eyes. Do not promise users more than it can hold, know the cost of upgrading, and keep your own copy of what matters.

items.q: Why do people discount being refused or suspended by a vendor?
options: Refusals are rare in practice
It feels personal and unlikely, though suspensions are often automated and appeals can be slow
Vendors always give advance notice
items.explain: A single flagged event can close an account that something important depends on. Know your recovery path and keep a second administrator.

items.q: A model name still appears in the provider's list but generation returns 'not found'. Which pattern is this?
options: A price change
Something you rely on being retired
A change of ownership
items.explain: A periodic test run, a version stamp and a probe of what the provider offers are how you find out before users do.

items.q: How does a change in a vendor's terms interact with an assurance you gave users?
options: Assurances are unaffected by vendor terms
A change of terms can turn a true assurance false overnight
Vendors notify users directly of changes
items.explain: Date-stamp what you checked and when, so that a later change is visible against a record.

items.q: Which kind of lock-in is the least visible in the code?
options: Data lock-in
Behavioural: instructions tuned against one model behave differently on another
Contract lock-in
items.explain: Nothing in the code reveals the dependence. It shows up when you switch and the outputs change, which is why a test set matters.

items.q: Why estimate each kind of lock-in in person-days?
options: It satisfies auditors
The largest number is the real lock-in, and any cell you cannot fill in shows you do not know what leaving involves
Person-days are the only unit vendors accept
items.explain: The biggest number is often not the one you expected, and an empty cell is a finding.

items.q: Which kinds of lock-in tend to be the expensive ones nobody budgets for?
options: Data and interface
Behaviour, workflow and skills, since they do not live in the code
Contract and data
items.explain: Version-controlled instructions, a written test set and a thin interface layer are mostly aimed at these.

items.q: Why can a database schema that rebuilds from migrations still be costly to move?
options: Migrations cannot be run on another host
It may rely on conventions specific to the current provider, such as its identity functions and role names
Schemas cannot be exported
items.explain: Moving would mean replacing that identity layer, which is real work and not just a copy.

items.q: Why is an exit plan that has never been run only a hope?
options: Plans are always out of date
Plans fail at details, such as an incomplete export or a forgotten dependency, that only a rehearsal finds
Vendors change their export formats weekly
items.explain: A rehearsal finds the surprises while they are cheap. Run by someone who did not write the plan, it also finds the gaps the author fills in from memory.

items.q: What makes a rehearsal more useful than reading through the plan?
options: It is quicker to complete
A real slice, run in order by someone else with a stopwatch, reveals gaps and true durations
It requires fewer people
items.explain: Write down every surprise. Reaching the verification step on a slice gives you most of the information.

items.q: What is the relationship between a backup and an exit plan?
options: They are unrelated
Both are claims proven only by doing them, and restoring a backup rehearses half of an exit
A backup replaces the need for an exit plan
items.explain: A backup you have never restored is a file you believe contains your data. Restoring to a scratch location is the cheapest rehearsal there is.

items.q: What does an abstraction layer around a vendor reduce the cost of?
options: Retuning instructions for a new model
Changing the plumbing, since vendor-specific calls are confined to one place
Retraining the team
items.explain: It leaves the cost of changing behaviour untouched. A thick layer that pretends to cover both creates a false sense of safety.

items.q: A layer reports a uniform 'tokens used', but one vendor reports reasoning tokens separately. What happened?
options: The vendor made an error
The abstraction leaked: the vendors did not mean quite the same thing, and spend could be undercounted
Tokens are not comparable between vendors
items.explain: A layer cannot present a uniform interface to something that is not uniform. Its job is to confine the differences.

items.q: Why is 'an abstraction with one working implementation' described as a guess?
options: One implementation is always insufficient
Whether it works is proven only when a second vendor actually runs behind it
Abstractions need at least three implementations by definition
items.explain: Untested adapters are claims, not capabilities. One real call through a second vendor is the test.

items.q: Is an open-weight model the same as open source?
options: Yes, open-weight models are always open source
No, the weights are downloadable but the licence may limit who can use them and how
Only for models from European labs
items.explain: Licences differ between families and versions. Read the one that applies to what you intend.

items.q: Which risk does running your own model remove?
options: Hardware cost
A provider silently changing or retiring the model, or refusing your region
The need for evaluation
items.explain: You choose the version and it stays put. You also take on hardware, operations, updates, security, evaluation and the safeguards the provider used to supply.

items.q: What is the practical position on self-hosting for a small project with one maintainer?
options: Self-host immediately to avoid vendor risk
Keep the code able to point at a model you host, as an option, without hosting one today
Avoid hosted models entirely
items.explain: The door is preserved at the cost of a configuration setting. It is an option rather than a plan, and the distinction matters.

items.q: Why is the clause on data when the relationship ends so important?
options: It determines the price of leaving
It decides whether an exit plan can succeed: whether you can export, in what form, and for how long
It controls which country's law applies
items.explain: Also check suspension grounds: a suspended account cannot export anything.

items.q: What does a liability cap usually mean for a free service?
options: The vendor pays for any loss in full
What you can recover is limited, often to what you paid, which may be very little
The cap is waived for free services
items.explain: Assume that a serious failure will cost you more than you can recover.

items.q: Why is an account registered to one person's email and phone a dependency?
options: Personal email is less secure
If that person is unreachable or leaves, the account and its recovery route go with them
Vendors charge more for personal accounts
items.explain: Use a role-based contact address, have a second administrator, and know the recovery process before you need it.

items.q: Why date what you read in a vendor's terms?
options: Dates are required by the vendor
Terms change, and a dated note lets you see later what moved and shows you did check
Older terms always apply to existing customers
items.explain: Record the vendor, plan, date, the answers to the key questions and what you do not know.

items.q: What is a correlated failure?
options: A failure that occurs twice in a row
Failures of things you thought were independent that share a cause, such as the same cloud, account or person
A failure that appears in the logs of two systems
items.explain: Two vendors that share a cloud do not protect you from that cloud. Independence is harder to establish than it looks.

items.q: Why does a backup held by the same vendor as the data give limited protection?
options: Same-vendor backups are always corrupted
It protects against a mistake but fails together with the vendor, so a copy elsewhere is needed
Vendors do not allow restoring their own backups
items.explain: A copy under a different account, ideally a different provider, is among the cheapest reductions available.

items.q: Why write exit triggers in advance?
options: Regulators require them
Otherwise the decision is made in the middle of a failure with the least information and the most pressure
Triggers make leaving automatic
items.explain: The point is not that you will leave when one occurs, but that the question gets asked on a schedule you chose.
